comments.author: etatoby
comments.story_title: Writing a Compiler in Go
comments.why_zh: 介绍把 text/template 的 parser 作为写编译器的范本。
comments.quote_zh: 作为入门，我推荐 Rob Pike 的演讲 "Lexical Scanning in Go"
comments.text_zh: 我想提一下，Go 编译器及相关工具中的绝大部分（即使不是全部）都是用 Go 本身写的，代码质量高且开源，可以在标准库的 "go" 包中找到：[LINK] 我建议把它当作自己写编译器的模板，因为它用的是地道的 Go 写法（最初由语言创造者编写），并且清晰地按抽象边界拆分（"scanner"、"parser"、"ast" 等包）。"text/template/parse" 包里还有一个更小、更简单的 parser，用来解析 "text/template" 和 "html/template" 中的模板语言。作为入门，我推荐 Rob Pike 的演讲 "Lexical Scanning in Go"：[VIDEO]
comments.text: I would like to mention that most, if not all, of the Go compiler and related utilities is written in Go itself, with high quality, open source code that can be found in the "go" package of the standard library: [LINK] I would recommend using that as a template for one's own compiler, because it's written in idiomatic Go (originally by the language creators) and is cleanly split across abstraction boundaries (packages "scanner", "parser", "ast", and so on.) There's also a smaller, simpler parser in the "text/template/parse" package, that is used to parse the templating languages in "text/template" and "html/template". As an introduction to it, I recommend the talk "Lexical Scanning in Go" by Rob Pike: [VIDEO]

comments.author: sapiogram
comments.story_title: Go: What we got right, what we got wrong
comments.quote_zh: 就像这个 2011 年的演讲[1]，它演示了用 goroutine 和 channel 实现经典的协程代码模式。
comments.text_zh: > 我认为 Go 花了很长时间在暗示 goroutine 是某种语言层面的特殊魔法，但我觉得现在大家都知道了，它们本质上是一个非常好的 green thread 实现，能够利用一些内部知识来做最优调度，以避免上下文切换。我花了好一阵子才想明白这一点，而当我内部指出这一点时，遭到了 Go 团队很多反驳。这条评论让我深感着迷，因为每次我回头去读/看 Rob Pike 等人早期的 Go 资料时，我都有同样的感觉，但我从没真正听到有人把它明确表达出来。我一直想，他们不至于对 PL 理论和历史那么无知吧？或者也许 Rob Pike 本人是，但他的团队肯定更清楚吧？真的感觉他们以为自己是在造线程与协程之间的某种特殊混合体，结合两者的优点。就像这个 2011 年的演讲[1]，它演示了用 goroutine 和 channel 实现经典的协程代码模式。但随着时间的推移，goroutine 变成了完全抢占式的，它们的编程模型现在与线程完全相同。根据我的经验，把它们当协程用只会带来痛苦（读作：数据竞争）。它们确实比 OS 线程快，但到这一步那只是实现细节。你觉得他们最终是什么时候意识到，自己是在重新发明 Java 十年前创造又废弃的同一套 green thread？[1] [VIDEO]
comments.text: > I think Go spent a lot of time implying that goroutines were some sort of special language magic, but I think everybody knows now that they are basically a really good implementation of green threads that can take advantage of some internal knowledge to do optimal scheduling to avoid context switches. It took me a while to work this out, and I got a lot of pushback from the go team when I pointed this out internally. This comment deeply fascinates me, because I get the same feeling every time I go back and read/watch early Go resources from Rob Pike and others, but I've never actually heard it articulated before. I've always thought that surely they weren't that ignorant about PL theory and history? Or maybe Rob Pike himself was, but surely his team knew better? It really feels like they thought they were making some special hybrid between threads and coroutines, combining the advantages of both. Like this 2011 talk[1] which demonstrated a classic coroutine code pattern implemented with goroutines and channels. But as time went on, goroutines became fully pre-emptive, and their programming model is now identical to threads. Using them as coroutines only leads to misery (read: data races) in my experience. They're faster than OS threads, sure, but that's an implementation detail at this point. When do you think they eventually realized they were re-inventing the same green threads Java had created and scrapped 10 years earlier? [1] [VIDEO]
